meaning: Back-up protection is secondary protection intended to operate when the primary protection fails to clear a fault or detect an abnormal condition in the required time.
studyNote: It provides another protective layer when the expected first device or breaker cannot or does not operate as intended.

meaning: A cartridge fuse link contains one or more fuse elements inside a cartridge, normally with arc-extinguishing material and terminations.
studyNote: It is the replaceable current-interrupting part used in cartridge-fuse systems.
distinction: A fuse is the complete device; the fuse link is the replaceable part and the fuse element is the part designed to melt.

meaning: A circuit-breaker is a switching device that can make and carry normal load current and can automatically interrupt specified abnormal currents, such as short-circuit current, under predetermined conditions.
studyNote: Unlike a fuse, it opens mechanically and can normally be reset after the fault is cleared, subject to the device's condition and instructions.
distinction: A circuit-breaker provides overcurrent functions; an RCD responds to residual current. An RCBO combines both functions.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide lists circuit-breakers among devices used for overload and short-circuit protection and distinguishes those functions from residual-current protection.

meaning: Danger is the risk of injury arising from electrical effects such as shock, fire, burns, arcing or explosion, and—within the stated scope—certain hazardous mechanical movement controlled electrically.
studyNote: The definition is about risk of injury, not merely the presence of electricity. Protective and emergency-switching measures are intended to control the relevant danger.

meaning: Design current (Ib) is the current a circuit is expected to carry in normal service.
studyNote: It is a design input used when selecting conductor current-carrying capacity and protective-device ratings.
distinction: Ib is the expected load current; Iz is conductor current-carrying capacity; In is commonly used for a device's rated current.

meaning: A disconnector is a mechanical switching device that, when open, satisfies the requirements for the isolating function.
studyNote: Its defining feature is safe isolation in the open position, not ordinary load switching.
distinction: A switch-disconnector can both perform normal switching and meet the isolating requirements of a disconnector.

meaning: Discrimination, also called selectivity, is coordination so one protective device operates in preference to another device connected in series.
studyNote: The aim is to isolate the affected part while avoiding unnecessary operation of upstream protection when the coordinated conditions are met.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide notes that time-delayed RCDs may be needed to provide selectivity with other RCDs.

meaning: Earth fault current is current caused by a low-impedance fault between a line conductor and an exposed-conductive-part or protective conductor.
studyNote: It flows through the earth-fault return path and must be cleared by the applicable fault-protection arrangement.
distinction: Earth fault current is one kind of fault current; short-circuit current is defined for a low-impedance fault between live conductors at different potentials.

meaning: Earth fault loop impedance (Zs) is the total impedance around the complete earth-fault current path, from the point of fault through the protective return path, source and line conductor back to the fault.
studyNote: Zs limits the earth fault current available to operate protective devices, so it is central to checking automatic disconnection where that method is used.
distinction: Earth-electrode resistance is only one possible part of the loop; Zs is the impedance of the complete loop.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide uses Zs in final-circuit limits and testing, and its test section distinguishes external loop impedance Ze from circuit earth-fault loop impedance.

meaning: A fault is an abnormal circuit condition in which current takes an unintended path, commonly because insulation has failed or been bridged.
studyNote: Fault conditions are distinguished from normal overload because the circuit is no longer electrically sound in the intended way.

meaning: Fault current is any current that results from a fault.
studyNote: It is the broad category; earth fault current and short-circuit current are more specific fault-current types.

meaning: A fuse is the complete protective device that interrupts excessive current by melting one or more specially designed fuse elements after the relevant current-time condition is reached.
studyNote: Operation is destructive to the fuse link, which must be replaced or renewed before the circuit can be put back into service.
distinction: The fuse is the complete device; the fuse link is the replaceable part; the fuse element is the part that melts.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide lists appropriate fuse standards among current overload and short-circuit protective-device options.

meaning: A fuse carrier is the movable part of a fuse that holds and carries the fuse link.
studyNote: It is a mechanical component of the fuse assembly, not the current-melting element itself.

meaning: The fuse element is the deliberately fusible part of a fuse that melts when the fuse operates.
studyNote: Its melting opens the current path and is the physical operating principle of the fuse.

meaning: A fuse link is the replaceable part of a fuse that contains the fuse element or elements and must be replaced or renewed after operation.
studyNote: It is the service-replacement portion of the complete fuse device.

meaning: Isolation is the safety function of separating all or a defined part of an installation from every source of electrical energy.
studyNote: It is used to establish a safe state for work or maintenance and must account for every relevant source, including alternative supplies where present.
distinction: Isolation is a safety function; functional switching is routine operational control.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide says safe isolation is vital and gives current requirements for means of isolation at the origin, for circuits and items of equipment, including identification and securing in the open position.

meaning: Overcurrent is current above the applicable rated value; for a conductor, the reference value is its current-carrying capacity.
studyNote: Overcurrent is the broad category that includes overload and fault-related excessive current.
distinction: An overload occurs in an electrically sound circuit; a short-circuit current is caused by a fault.

meaning: Overcurrent detection is the process of determining that circuit current has exceeded a chosen threshold for a specified time.
studyNote: Protective devices use current magnitude and time characteristics to decide when an overcurrent condition requires operation.

meaning: Overload current is an overcurrent in a circuit that is otherwise electrically sound.
studyNote: Typical overload is caused by excessive demand rather than an insulation failure or low-impedance fault path.
distinction: A short-circuit or earth-fault current is fault current; overload current occurs without an electrical fault in the circuit.

meaning: Prospective fault current (Ipf/PFC) is the current that would flow at a particular point if a fault of negligible impedance occurred between the specified conductors or between a live conductor and an exposed-conductive-part.
studyNote: Protective equipment at that point must have suitable making and breaking capability for the fault level that can occur.
distinction: It is a prospective value for a hypothetical low-impedance fault, not the normal design current of the circuit.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide links protective-device breaking capacity to prospective fault current and describes how prospective fault current is measured or obtained for verification.

meaning: Protective separation is separation between circuits using double insulation, reinforced insulation, or basic insulation together with protective screening.
studyNote: It provides a higher safety separation than simple separation because an additional protective measure beyond basic insulation is present.
distinction: Simple separation uses basic insulation only.

meaning: Rated current is the current value assigned to equipment or a device for specification under defined operating conditions.
studyNote: It is a nameplate or design rating, not necessarily the current actually flowing at a particular moment.
distinction: Do not confuse rated current with design current or conductor current-carrying capacity.

meaning: Residual current is the algebraic sum of the currents in all live conductors at a point in the installation.
studyNote: In a healthy balanced path, outgoing and returning currents largely cancel; a non-zero residual indicates some current is returning by another path.
distinction: Residual current is the measured imbalance quantity; an RCD is the device that responds to it.

meaning: An RCD is a switching device, or association of devices, that opens contacts when residual current reaches the operating condition specified for the device.
studyNote: Its core function is residual-current protection. Depending on the device type and circuit, that may provide fault protection, additional protection or fire-related protection, but an RCD does not automatically provide overcurrent protection.
distinction: An RCCB provides residual-current protection without integral overcurrent protection; an RCBO combines residual-current and overcurrent functions.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide gives current RCD applications, types, ratings and selection considerations and distinguishes RCBOs from RCCBs. It also shows the current user test notice requirement.

meaning: An RCBO is a residual-current operated circuit-breaker that also provides overload and/or short-circuit protection.
studyNote: It combines the residual-current function of an RCD with overcurrent protection in one device, so it can protect an individual circuit against both categories of condition when correctly selected.
distinction: An RCCB has no integral overcurrent protection; an RCBO does.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide explicitly describes RCBOs as devices combining circuit-breaker and residual-current functions and gives current selection information.

meaning: An RCCB is a residual-current operated switching device without integral overload or short-circuit protection.
studyNote: It must therefore be used with suitable overcurrent protection provided elsewhere in the circuit or assembly.
distinction: An RCBO includes overcurrent protection; an RCCB does not.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide distinguishes RCCBs from RCBOs and shows common consumer-unit arrangements using RCCBs with separate overcurrent protective devices.

meaning: Residual operating current is the residual current that causes an RCD to operate under the specified conditions.
studyNote: It describes the RCD's residual-current operating threshold, not its normal load-current rating.
distinction: Do not confuse residual operating current with rated current carried by the RCD or circuit.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide discusses RCD residual-current ratings, including 30 mA additional protection and other ratings for particular functions.

meaning: Short-circuit current is an overcurrent caused by a low-impedance fault between live conductors that normally have a voltage difference between them.
studyNote: Because it can be very large, protective devices must interrupt it within their rated breaking capability and required operating time.
distinction: Overload current occurs in an electrically sound circuit; short-circuit current is caused by a fault.

meaning: A surge protective device (SPD) limits transient overvoltage and diverts surge current using at least one non-linear component.
studyNote: Its purpose is to reduce damaging transient voltage stress on the installation and connected equipment; it is not an overcurrent protective device for normal overloads or short circuits.
distinction: The {534} marker means the supplied historical definition applies within Section 534.

currentGuide.note: The 2026 On-Site Guide explains transient-overvoltage protection, Type 1/2/3 SPD locations, coordination and the importance of keeping connecting conductors short.

meaning: A switch is a mechanical device intended to make, carry and break current under normal circuit conditions and to carry specified abnormal current for a stated time; some switches can make but not break short-circuit current.
studyNote: The definition does not by itself mean the device is suitable for isolation.
distinction: A switch-disconnector is a switch that also meets the isolating requirements in the open position.

meaning: A switch-disconnector combines normal switching capability with the isolating performance required of a disconnector when open.
studyNote: It can therefore be used for switching and, where correctly selected and installed, for the isolation function.
